Bane

/BAYN/ - rhymes with rain · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Bane means a source of serious and lasting harm, ruin, or trouble.

Potholes are the bane of the city's delivery riders, bending rims and snapping spokes all winter long.

Worked Example

Ask any touring cellist about dry air. It creeps into the case overnight, opens seams along the instrument's ribs, and deadens the tone of wood that sang the evening before. Players tape hygrometers inside their cases and carry humidifiers the size of soap bars, and still the cracks come every January.

Bane is the exact word for what dry air is to them, because a bane is a source of lasting harm, ruin, or trouble — not one bad night but a standing enemy a whole trade organizes its life around. A nuisance merely irritates; a curse implies doom from on high. A bane is the everyday, named tormentor that keeps doing real damage.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

curse: doom with a supernatural flavor; a bane is the everyday named tormentor of a life or trade

torment: the ongoing pain itself; a bane is its source

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

blessing: a source of steady good

godsend: the welcome arrival that saves the day

Where it sits · the scale of the harm done — nuisance → bane → scourge

nuisance vs. bane: A nuisance costs you minutes and patience — the dripping tap, the squeaky hinge — and it ruins nothing.

scourge vs. bane: Scourge goes further than bane — a bane wears down one gardener or one shipping line; a scourge lays waste to whole regions at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bane

Root — bane: slayer, killer (Old English bana)

Put it together

Put it together: There is nothing to peel off here: bane came down from Old English bana, "slayer," as a single piece. A thousand years softened it from the killer himself to the thing that ruins you — the modern bane does its killing slowly, by wear.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Old English bana meant a killer outright, and the word survives today only tucked inside old plant names — wolfsbane and henbane, "wolf-killer" and "hen-killer," poison plants named with the same word. Those are the word itself in old costume, not relatives you can peel it down to.

Strength Check

Word Choice

literary / rueful

Bane names a standing enemy, and it loves the possessive: the bane of my existence, the bane of every commuter. For devastation at regional scale, reach for scourge; for a mere irritation, nuisance. Its neighbor in this unit is blight — a blight spreads through what it ruins, while a bane just keeps standing on your road.
